newsitem.title: UK: Stick to Europe amid financial market turmoil - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Stick to Europe amid financial market turmoil - analysts.

text.p: European financial markets offer a haven for investors frazzled by last week's trading chaos as U.S. stocks and bonds are becoming increasingly too hot to handle, analysts said on Monday.
European markets will continue to flourish in an environment of low interest rates while speculation that U.S. rates are set to rise will cast a pall over markets there, analysts said.
"I would be selling U.S. equities now," said Julian Jessop of Nikko Europe in London. "I think the Greenspan message was important. He is preparing the ground for a rate rise."

Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan set world financial markets alight on Friday when he said the Fed must be wary when "irrational exuberance" unduly escalates asset values as that could end up damaging the economy.
He also said interest rate changes took time to feed into the economy, which meant the Fed often had to tighten or ease before action was evident to the public.

Markets interpreted Greenspan's comments as meaning a rise in U.S. interest rates may be on the horizon and recent speculation that rates might in fact be heading down was well off the mark, analysts said. Debt and stock markets plunged.

Weaker-than-expected U.S. jobs data later on Friday eased some of the losses but analysts here said the message from Greenspan was clear -- the rally in U.S. equities all year and the rebound in Treasuries since September were nearing an end.

Richard Urwin, head of economic research at Gartmore, the investment management subsidiary of Natwest Markets here, said both U.S. bond and stock markets were beginning to look overextended, even before Greenspan's comments.
In Europe, equity markets have rallied this year but not to the heady heights reached by U.S. stock markets, Urwin said.
"Equity markets relative to bonds in Europe were not looking as extended. That was true for both the UK and continental Euorpe and indeed Japanese equities looked cheap against bonds," he said.

"All those measures will be staying pretty much the same," Urwin said. "Unless you have a very short-term timeframe I don't think you should be changing your views based on half a sentence from Alan Greenspan," he said.
Jessop, Nikko Europe's chief European economist, favours bond markets in Europe, with equities restrained by weak growth.

"The textbook economic view tells us that equities are moved by two things, corporate earnings and interest rates," said Jessop. "Obviously they'll benefit on the interest rate side but they'll suffer on the corporate earnings."
Michael O'Hanlon, chief international economist at PaineWebber in London, said however the textbook economic view of equities no longer held true for the U.S.
The major restructuring in U.S. companies over the last few years which has made them leaner, meaner and better able to compete will continue to fatten earnings, he said.
"I wouldn't be overly cautious about stocks at this point," he said, putting a three-month target on the Dow Jones Industrial average of 6,800 after its 6,381.94 close on Friday.
While both stock and bond markets in Europe will benefit from low interest rates, politics could hijack the bond rally.
Uncertainties about European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) could restrain bond gains in 1997 as investors become cautious on EMU starting in 1999 and under strict criteria.

Longer term, equities could benefit more substantially under EMU than bonds as corporate credit ratings get upgraded beyond their sovereign ceiling. The whole euro area is likely to receive a AAA credit rating giving companies in countries with lower ratings the chance to be upgraded.
"You could well have a situation where corporates are rated higher than sovereigns and that becomes very important for why one can assume stocks can do very well relative to bonds," he said.
